title: Investing · Episode 1
chapters: Moats: why some companies stay on top
What is a business worth? Valuation explained

units.t: Investing. Episode one.
In this episode: Risk and return, How the stock market works, Moats: why some companies stay on top and What is a business worth? Valuation explained.
Part one. Risk and return.
There is no such thing as a high return with no risk.
Understanding why is the first real lesson of investing.
No free returns.
The risk-return trade-off is the closest thing investing has to a law of nature.
Money in a government-guaranteed bank account is very unlikely to lose value in dollar terms, so it pays a modest interest rate.
Shares in companies can fall sharply, so investors demand the prospect of a higher long-run return to hold them.
If an asset offered high returns with no risk, everyone would buy it until its price rose and its future return shrank.
That is why any offer of 'high returns, no risk' should set off alarm bells.
What risk means.
Most people think of risk as losing money, and that matters.
Professionals use a broader meaning: uncertainty about outcomes.
A term deposit paying 4 per cent has little uncertainty.
A share fund might return 25 per cent one year and lose 15 per cent the next.
That swing is volatility: how widely and how often a price moves.
Cash barely moves.
The main Australian share index fell roughly half between late 2007 and early 2009, and more than a third in about a month in early 2020.
Both times it recovered, but anyone forced to sell near the bottom locked in heavy losses.
The asset classes.
Investments are grouped into asset classes that behave in broadly similar ways.
Cash, such as savings accounts and term deposits, is the most stable but usually earns the least.
Fixed interest, mainly bonds, pays regular interest and tends to be steadier than shares.
Property can deliver rent and capital growth but is lumpy, costly to buy and sell, and can fall in value.
Shares, Australian and international, have historically delivered the highest long-run returns of the main classes, with the biggest swings.
Cash and bonds are often called defensive assets; property and shares are growth assets.
Time and temperament.
Your time horizon is how long until you need the money.
Over ten or twenty years, diversified share portfolios have historically been far more likely to end up ahead, though that is a pattern from the past, not a guarantee.
Money for a house deposit in two years usually belongs somewhere stable.
Money you won't touch for decades, like much of your super, can generally afford more growth assets.
Two more limits apply.
Risk tolerance is emotional: can you watch your balance drop 30 per cent without panicking?
Risk capacity is financial: could you afford that drop?
A nervous young worker has high capacity; a brave retiree drawing on savings has less.
Real returns, real plans.
A 5 per cent return sounds decent, but if prices rise 4 per cent, your real return is only about 1 per cent, and after tax it may be near zero.
So cash is not truly risk-free over long periods.
Australia's Reserve Bank targets inflation of 2-3 per cent on average, which roughly halves the value of a dollar every 25 to 35 years.
Think in buckets.
Emergency money belongs in cash, and short-term goals suit cash or conservative options.
Long-term money, like super, can usually lean towards growth.
Check which option your fund has you in.
This is general information, not personal advice; speak to a licensed financial adviser, and see ASIC's Moneysmart for free guidance.
The key idea: Investments that can earn higher returns usually come with a higher chance of losses along the way.
Part two. How the stock market works.
What you're actually buying when you buy a share, why prices jump around, and how ordinary people build wealth with it.
What a share is.
A share, or stock, is a small slice of ownership in a company.
If a company has a million shares and you own 1,000, you own 0.
1 per cent of it, including a claim on 0.
1 per cent of its future profits.
Companies sell shares to raise money without borrowing, and shareholders can usually vote on big decisions.
If the company does well, your slice becomes more valuable; if it fails, it can become worthless.
A stock exchange is a marketplace where shares are traded.
Australia's main one is the ASX, formed in 1987 from the merger of earlier state exchanges.
Most trading is electronic.
A company's first public sale of shares is an initial public offering, or IPO.
After that, investors trade with each other, and the company doesn't get the money from those trades.
What moves prices.
If more people want to buy than sell, the price rises.
Underneath, buyers are betting on future profits.
Prices react to earnings, scandals, interest rates and the economy.
In the short term, fear and excitement drive them; in the long run, they tend to follow real profits.
A rising market is a bull market, and a fall of 20 per cent or more from a peak is a bear market.
Markets fell sharply in 1987, in the 2008–09 financial crisis, and in early 2020, when the ASX lost over a third of its value in about a month.
Broad markets have historically recovered, though it can take years, and past performance guarantees nothing.
How investors earn.
There are two main ways to make money from shares.
If the price rises and you sell for more than you paid, that's a capital gain.
And many companies pay part of their profits to shareholders as dividends, usually twice a year in Australia.
Australian companies often attach franking credits to dividends.
They represent company tax already paid, and can reduce the tax you owe.
Reinvesting dividends to buy more shares is a powerful way to compound growth.
Index funds, not gambling.
An index tracks a group of stocks.
The ASX 200 tracks the 200 largest companies on the ASX; the S and P 500 tracks 500 large US companies.
An index fund, often an exchange-traded fund, ETF, simply buys every company in an index, giving you a tiny slice of hundreds of businesses at low cost.
Most professional fund managers fail to beat their index over the long term, once fees are included.
Holding a broad index fund for decades is very different from day-trading or chasing tips on social media.
Studies consistently find most day traders lose money over time, after costs.
Invest for the long term, diversify, keep fees low, don't try to time the market, and never invest money you might need soon.
This is general information, not personal advice; a licensed adviser can help.
Rules of the game.
A fair market needs everyone to have access to the same important information.

Under the ASX's continuous disclosure rules, a listed company must immediately announce anything a reasonable person would expect to affect its share price materially, such as a big new contract, a profit downgrade or a takeover offer.
If news is about to break, the company can ask for a trading halt so no one trades on half the story.
Buying or selling shares using price-sensitive information that isn't public, or tipping someone else off, is insider trading.
It's a serious crime in Australia, carrying up to 15 years' jail, and the corporate regulator, ASIC, investigates suspicious trades.
The key idea: A share is a small slice of ownership in a company, bought and sold on exchanges like the ASX.
Part three. Moats: why some companies stay on top.
Most successful businesses attract copycats that eat away their profits.
A few seem untouchable for decades.
The difference is what investors call a moat.
The castle and the moat.
Picture a medieval castle full of treasure.
The treasure is a company's profits, and every competitor would love to storm the walls.
Investor Warren Buffett popularised the idea that the best businesses are protected by a wide economic moat.
In ordinary markets, high profits are a signal to others.
If a cafe makes a fortune, new cafes open next door, prices fall and profits shrink back to normal.
Economists call this competition doing its job.
A moat interrupts that process, letting a company earn unusually high returns for many years.
Spotting a real moat is hard, and mistaking temporary success for a lasting advantage is one of the most common errors in business and investing.
Locked-in customers.
A telephone is useless if you are the only owner, and more useful with every new person who joins.
This is a network effect.
Card payment networks are a classic case: shops accept a card because customers carry it, and customers carry it because shops accept it.
A better rival struggles to get everyone to switch together, which helps explain why digital markets end up dominated by one or two giants, and why regulators watch them closely.
Switching costs work differently.
Moving a large company's accounting software means years of records, trained staff and connected systems.
Changing banks means updating direct debits.
Businesses deepen these costs with loyalty schemes and bundles.
When convenience turns into dependence, a company has the most power over price.
Cost and intangible edges.
Some companies win by producing more cheaply than rivals.
A huge retailer can negotiate lower supplier prices, spread advertising across thousands of stores and fund efficient logistics.
Economists call these economies of scale.
Location can matter too: a quarry near a city has a lasting advantage, because rock is heavy and costly to transport.
But a rival's cleverer method can erase a cost advantage.
Other moats are intangible.
A patent gives an inventor exclusive rights for a limited time, usually up to 20 years, in exchange for disclosing how the invention works.
Drug revenues can fall sharply when a major patent expires and cheaper generics arrive.
Government licences can limit a market to a few operators.
A trusted brand can allow higher prices, though familiarity alone does not guarantee pricing power.
Moats can dry up.
History is full of companies that looked unbeatable.
In the late 2000s Nokia sold more mobile phones than anyone, and BlackBerry was the device of choice for business.
Within a few years touchscreen smartphones with app stores had pushed both aside.
Newspapers once held a powerful moat in classified advertising: to sell a car or find a job, you went to the paper with the most readers.
The internet drained that moat remarkably quickly.
These stories show moats are not permanent.
They need constant maintenance and are vulnerable to shifts that make the old advantage irrelevant.
A company that grows complacent behind its walls may not notice the water level falling.
Thinking like an analyst.
You can use moat thinking on any business, from a local bakery to a global tech giant.
Ask: if a well-funded competitor tried to copy this company tomorrow, what would stop them?
If the honest answer is not much, high profits are unlikely to last.
Analysts look for evidence such as steady returns on capital over many years, loyal customers and the ability to raise prices without losing sales.
A great company is not automatically a great investment if its share price already reflects all that strength.
This is general information rather than financial advice, and moneysmart.
gov.
au has helpful guidance if you are thinking about investing.
The key idea: A moat is any lasting advantage that stops rivals from competing away a company's profits.
Part four. What is a business worth? Valuation explained.
Two experts can look at the same company and arrive at prices billions apart.
Valuation is part maths, part judgement, and understanding it changes how you see every price tag in the market.
Price versus value.
Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
Warren Buffett, a student of the investor Benjamin Graham, put it that way.
A price is a fact, such as the latest share price or an agreed sale.
Value is an estimate of what the business is really worth to its owners, and estimates differ.
A buyer and a seller can disagree sharply, both in good faith.
Most serious valuation rests on one idea: a business is worth the cash it will generate for its owners over its remaining life.
Everything else, from complex spreadsheets to rules of thumb, is a way of estimating that cash and what it is worth today.
Money today beats tomorrow.
Would you rather have 100 dollars today or in a year?
Almost everyone says today.
Money in hand can be invested, it avoids the risk of a broken promise, and inflation can erode what future money buys.
So analysts discount future amounts back to the present.
If you could earn 10 per cent elsewhere, 100 dollars in a year is worth about 90.
91 dollars today, because that sum grows to 100 at 10 per cent.
This is the base of discounted cash flow, DCF.
An analyst forecasts the free cash flow in each future year, meaning cash left after running the business and making necessary investments.
Each year is discounted to today's dollars, then the results are added up.
Discount rate and risk.
Nobody can forecast forever, so analysts model five or ten years in detail, then add one terminal value for everything after.
A common method treats the business as growing steadily for ever: next year's cash flow divided by the discount rate minus the growth rate.
Often this is most of the total.
The discount rate is where judgement and risk enter.
It is the return investors require for backing this business instead of another.
A stable utility earns a lower rate than an uncertain young technology firm.
Small changes matter.
One million dollars of cash flow growing 2 per cent for ever is worth 12.
5 million at a 10 per cent rate, but about 14.
3 million at 9 per cent.
Comparison and debt.
DCF is rigorous but laborious, so analysts also use multiples, much like valuing a house from recent sales nearby.
The price to earnings ratio compares share price with profit per share.
Enterprise value to EBITDA compares the whole business, debt included, with earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.
If similar firms trade at ten times EBITDA, a business earning five million might be worth about fifty million.
Multiples are quick and market-based, but if the whole market is overpriced they copy the error.
Enterprise value is the whole operating business.
Equity value is roughly that minus net debt, debt less spare cash.
An 800,000 dollar house with a 500,000 dollar mortgage gives you only 300,000 of equity.
Garbage in, garbage out.
Valuation models look precise, with numbers to the last dollar, but they rest on forecasts of growth, margins and risk that nobody can know.
As the example showed, a one percentage point change in the discount rate can shift a valuation by more than ten per cent.
The long-term growth rate has a similar effect.
Careful analysts therefore present a range, test pessimistic and optimistic scenarios, and check the answer against multiples.

Many experienced investors also want a margin of safety, another idea linked to Graham: buy only when the price is comfortably below their estimate of value, so that errors in their assumptions do not ruin them.
The key idea: The price of a business is what someone pays; its value is an estimate of the cash it can produce for its owners.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why don't low-risk investments usually offer high returns?
Answer. Because demand would push prices up and returns down.
Question two. What does owning a share mean?
Answer. You own a small part of the company.
Question three. In business, what is an economic moat?
Answer. A lasting edge that protects profits.
Question four. According to most serious valuation, what is a business worth?
Answer. The cash it will produce for its owners over time.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
